This policy is rare in Europe and Asia, where citizenship is usually based on parentage (jus sanguinis).

    People also ask
    What countries do birthright citizenship?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Approximately 30-40 countries, mostly in the Americas, offer unconditional birthright citizenship (jus soli or "right of soil"), which grants automatic citizenship to almost anyone born within their territory, regardless of parentage. Key nations include the United States, Canada, Mexico, Argentina, Brazil, and most of South America/Caribbean. 
    Key Countries with Unconditional Birthright Citizenship
    Unconditional jus soli is relatively rare globally, with the highest concentration found in the Western Hemisphere. 
    • North America: United States, Canada, Mexico. 
    • Central America & Caribbean: Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Belize, Costa Rica, Cuba, Dominica, El Salvador, Grenada, Guatemala, Honduras, Jamaica, Panama, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Trinidad and Tobago. 
    • South America: Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Ecuador, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, Venezuela. 
    • Other/Limited Examples: Chad, Gambia, Lesotho, Fiji, Pakistan (some, with restrictions). 
    Contextual Notes
    • Jus Soli vs. Jus Sanguinis: Most countries in Europe, Asia, and Africa follow jus sanguinis ("right of blood"), meaning citizenship is inherited from parents, not by place of birth. 
    • Conditional Citizenship: Some nations allow citizenship by birth only if specific criteria are met (e.g., parents are legal residents), such as France, Germany, and the UK. 
    • Regional Trends: The prevalence in the Americas is a legacy of colonialism, aimed at boosting population size.

      Is Canada a birthright citizenship?
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Yes, Canada has birthright citizenship, known as jus soli (right of soil). Almost any child born in Canada automatically becomes a Canadian citizen at birth, regardless of the parents' nationality or immigration status. The only exception is children born to foreign diplomats or diplomatic staff. 
      Key Details on Canadian Birthright Citizenship:
      • Automatic Status:
        Birthright citizenship is automatic upon birth within Canadian territory, including airspaces. 
      • Exceptions:
        Children born to foreign diplomats, consular officers, or employees of foreign governments working in Canada are not automatically citizens. 
      • Parents' Status:
        The immigration status (e.g., permanent resident, temporary worker, visitor) of the parents does not affect the child's citizenship status. 
      • Proof:
        The birth certificate issued by the province or territory serves as proof of citizenship. 
      • Citizenship by Descent:
        For children born outside Canada to at least one Canadian parent, citizenship is generally conferred at birth, though new regulations effective Dec 15, 2025, require parents born abroad to meet a "substantial connection" test. 
      While there has been public debate regarding "birth tourism"—where non-citizens travel to Canada to give birth—birthright citizenship remains a foundational component of Canadian immigration law.

        Do European countries have birthright citizenship?
        No country in the EU grants automatic and unconditional citizenship to children born on their territories to foreign citizens. In countries that provide for conditional ius soli, the most common condition is that parents should have resided in the country for a certain time before the child's birth.
